\chapter{Eleven to Fifteen}
\label{ch:mw-teens-to-fifteen}
\hlchaptermodality{37}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say and write eleven to fifteen in Marwadi, and name the one of them that does not rhyme with the rest.}

The five teens heard singly out of order, read printed, written from dictation, and sorted by the ending that four of them share.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[i]{\mw{इ} — the fourth standing vowel}

\label{lesson:MW-W37-i}



\begin{quote}
Say the line that closes a bargain — \emph{paisā le lo} — and write the \textbf{\mw{ि}} mark on any consonant you like.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the mark, standing on its own}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{इ}} — \emph{i} — the vowel with no consonant under it
\end{quote}

Since chapter 7 the hand has made \textbf{\mw{ि}}, the hook that leans in \emph{front} of the consonant it is read \emph{after}. A vowel that opens a word has nothing to lean on, so Devanagari gives it a letter that stands on the line by itself.

\textbf{\mw{आ}} was isolated in chapter 2, \textbf{\mw{ई}} in chapter 6, \textbf{\mw{ए}} in chapter 32 for the first number. \textbf{\mw{इ}} is the fourth, and eleven is what needs it.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Trace \textbf{\mw{इ}} three times. Write \textbf{\mw{ि}} beside it and say which of the two can begin a word on its own. Then look at \textbf{\mw{ई}} and mark the one stroke that separates the two standing letters.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
This is the first of the four signs the teens will ask for.

Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[igyārā]{Hear \emph{igyārā} — eleven}

\label{lesson:MW-C37-hear-igyaara}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{इ}}, the letter the last lesson stood up — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} run the numbered price exchange once, seller's figure and all — \textbf{R3}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{पैसा} \mw{ले} \mw{लो}} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{igyārā} — \textbf{eleven}
\end{quote}

The count so far stopped at \emph{das}, ten, and jumped to \emph{bīs}, twenty. This is the first of the nine words that fill the gap.

Say it in three beats: \emph{i-gyā-rā}. The middle beat carries a \textbf{gy} cluster that has to stay one sound, not two — the tongue is already at the palate for the \textbf{y} while the \textbf{g} is still closing.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/soas/}{Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[igyārā]{\mw{इग्यारा} — eleven on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C37-igyaara}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{igyārā} aloud before you look at it — \textbf{R1}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{इ}} + \textbf{\mw{ग्या}} + \textbf{\mw{रा}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{इग्यारा}} — \emph{igyārā} — eleven
\end{quote}

Three pieces, and only the first is new. \textbf{\mw{ग्या}} is \textbf{\mw{ग}} with its upright stem cut away and \textbf{\mw{या}} joined on behind it — the same virama \textbf{\mw{्}} you have been writing since chapter 4, doing the job it exists for: two consonants, one breath, no vowel between them.

\textbf{\mw{रा}} is chapter 1's \textbf{\mw{र}} with the \textbf{\mw{ा}} you have written more often than any other mark in this book.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Copy \textbf{\mw{इग्यारा}} once while looking. Then write the three pieces apart — \textbf{\mw{इ}}, \textbf{\mw{ग्या}}, \textbf{\mw{रा}} — and point at the stem that \textbf{\mw{ग}} gave up.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bārā]{Hear \emph{bārā} — twelve}

\label{lesson:MW-C37-hear-baara}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{इग्यारा}} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write the figures \textbf{\mw{०}}, \textbf{\mw{१}} and \textbf{\mw{२}} — \textbf{R3}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{do}, \textquotedblleft{}give\textquotedblright{}, and say which of its two jobs this is — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{bārā} — \textbf{twelve}
\end{quote}

Two is \emph{do}. Twelve is \emph{bārā}, and there is no \emph{do} in it — the \textbf{b} is what is left of an older word for two that Marwari kept only inside the teens. English does the same thing with \emph{two} and \emph{twelve}, where the \textbf{tw-} survives and the rest does not.

The ending \textbf{-ārā} is the one \emph{igyārā} had. From here to nineteen you will hear it again and again: the teens are a set that rhymes.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/soas/}{Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bārā]{\mw{बारा} — twelve on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C37-baara}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{bārā} before you look at it — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{दो}} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{बा}} + \textbf{\mw{रा}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{बारा}} — \emph{bārā} — twelve
\end{quote}

Two pieces, no new sign, and both halves take the same \textbf{\mw{ा}}. \textbf{\mw{ब}} came in with \emph{bīs}; \textbf{\mw{र}} has been in the hand since the first greeting.

Written beside \textbf{\mw{दो}}, the point the ear made is visible: twelve and two share one letter and nothing else.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Look at \textbf{\mw{बारा}}, cover it, wait five seconds, write it. Then write \textbf{\mw{इग्यारा}} under it and ring the \textbf{\mw{रा}} that ends both.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[terā]{Hear \emph{terā} — thirteen}

\label{lesson:MW-C37-hear-tera}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{बारा}} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{इ}}, five lessons back — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} run the six-turn numbered exchange once — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write the figures \textbf{\mw{३}}, \textbf{\mw{४}} and \textbf{\mw{५}} — \textbf{R3}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ākhrī} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{terā} — \textbf{thirteen}
\end{quote}

Three is \emph{tīn}. Thirteen is \emph{terā}: the \textbf{t} stays, the long \textbf{ī} flattens to \textbf{e}, and the teens ending arrives. Two beats, both short of effort — \emph{te-rā}.

You have now heard the pattern three times, and it is the pattern rather than the words that is worth holding: \textbf{a consonant off the small number, then -ārā or -erā}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/soas/}{Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[terā]{\mw{तेरा} — thirteen on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C37-tera}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{terā} before you look at it — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{igyārā}, five lessons back — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{आखरी}} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{ते}} + \textbf{\mw{रा}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{तेरा}} — \emph{terā} — thirteen
\end{quote}

The \textbf{\mw{े}} above \textbf{\mw{त}} is the mark chapter 7 taught and chapter 32 stood up as the letter \textbf{\mw{ए}}. Here it is doing its ordinary job again, riding on a consonant.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Write \textbf{\mw{तेरा}} from memory after five seconds covered. Then write \textbf{\mw{बारा}} and \textbf{\mw{इग्यारा}} beneath it and read the three down the page, ending in \textbf{\mw{रा}} each time.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[caudā]{Hear \emph{caudā} — fourteen}

\label{lesson:MW-C37-hear-chauda}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{तेरा}} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{इग्यारा}}, five lessons back — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write the figures \textbf{\mw{६}}, \textbf{\mw{७}} and \textbf{\mw{८}} — \textbf{R3}
  \item \emph{Recall:} ask \emph{kitṇo ākhrī bhāv doge?} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{caudā} — \textbf{fourteen}
\end{quote}

Four is \emph{chār}. Fourteen keeps the \textbf{ch} and then does something none of the others do: it ends \textbf{-dā}, not \textbf{-rā}.

That is worth marking rather than smoothing over. Three teens in a row have rhymed and the fourth breaks the rhyme, so this is the one in the set most likely to be misremembered as \emph{chaurā}. It is not.

The \textbf{au} is the diphthong of \emph{mausam}, the weather word from chapter 16 — the mouth already knows it.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/soas/}{Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[caudā]{\mw{चौदा} — fourteen on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C37-chauda}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{caudā} before you look at it — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{bārā}, five lessons back — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{कितणो} \mw{आखरी} \mw{भाव} \mw{दोगे}?} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{चौ}} + \textbf{\mw{दा}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{चौदा}} — \emph{caudā} — fourteen
\end{quote}

The \textbf{\mw{ौ}} is the mark \textbf{\mw{मौसम}} taught, and \textbf{\mw{द}} has been in the hand since \emph{do}. Nothing here is new; what is new is the pairing.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Write \textbf{\mw{चौदा}} from memory after five seconds. Then write \textbf{\mw{तेरा}} beside it and ring the two different last letters — \textbf{\mw{र}} and \textbf{\mw{द}} — so the eye records the break the ear heard.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pandarā]{Hear \emph{pandarā} — fifteen}

\label{lesson:MW-C37-hear-pandara}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{चौदा}} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{तेरा}}, five lessons back — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write the figure \textbf{\mw{९}} — \textbf{R3}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{बारा}} — \textbf{R2}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{pandarā} — \textbf{fifteen}
\end{quote}

Five is \emph{pāṅch}. Fifteen keeps the \textbf{p} and the nasal, and the \textbf{-arā} rhyme is back after fourteen broke it.

Three beats: \emph{pan-da-rā}. The nasal in the middle is the same one already in \emph{pāṅch} — the sound the anusvara writes.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/soas/}{Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pandarā]{\mw{पंदरा} — fifteen on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C37-pandara}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{pandarā} before you look at it — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{चौदा}}, five lessons back — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} run the final-price exchange once, all four turns — \textbf{R4}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{terā} — \textbf{R2}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{पं}} + \textbf{\mw{द}} + \textbf{\mw{रा}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{पंदरा}} — \emph{pandarā} — fifteen
\end{quote}

The dot over \textbf{\mw{प}} is the anusvara from chapter 3, the one \textbf{\mw{हां}} needed. There it nasalised a vowel; here it stands for a full \textbf{n} before \textbf{\mw{द}}. Same mark, and the letter after it decides what it sounds like.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Write \textbf{\mw{पंदरा}} from memory after five seconds. Then write \textbf{\mw{हां}} beside it and say what the same dot is doing in each.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Eleven to fifteen, heard and written}

\label{lesson:MW-R37-count-fifteen}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{पंदरा}} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{इ}}, the letter five lessons back stood up — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} read a printed ticket and say the figure on it aloud — \textbf{R3}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Five words, shuffled, with the chapter no longer giving the answer away.

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Hear the five named singly and out of order; say each back.
  \item Read the five printed and say each aloud.
  \item Write three of them from dictation, the choice named only as you write.
  \item Say the four that end \textbf{-\mw{रा}} and the one that does not, and say what its last letter is instead.
\end{enumerate}
